title: The Second Play
passages:
The drum screamed. Not a metaphor — the Marrow's winch, a salvaged capstan bolted to the keel and fed by a hydrogen cell that whined like a dying mosquito, was hauling two hundred kilos of unconscious diver through a vertical shaft of gray water, and the bearings had not been greased since the last storm season. Each revolution bit into the hull's ribs. Sol had the shutter cracked, one eye on the gate's red light, the other on the line disappearing through the moon pool. Dey sat lashed to the mast step, his chest hitching with the wet rattle of lungs that had traded their last clean breath for a child's life, fingers white-knuckled on a coil he could no longer work. Salas stood amidships, motionless, the line's bitter end wrapped twice around his forearm, the coil at his feet like a sleeping snake. He had not spoken since he broke surface fourteen months after the world wrote him off. Bayo Adisa was at the drum, bandaged hands finding the rhythm, shoulders squared against the surge that slammed the hull every twelve seconds.

Wren knelt at the comms console, slate cradled in her lap, the barnacled recorder from Salas's harness clipped to the input jack. The first play — Mara's voice, cool and precise, directing a diver to the second seal beneath Mercy General's pharmacy — had driven them here. One play left on the slate.

"Nia," she said into the mic. "Nia, hear me. Talk to me." Static. The carrier wave held, but the return was dead air. At thirty meters the scrubber canister had given up, the CO2 scrubbing media exhausted, and from there the clock was not depth or line speed but the acid already eating her blood. Wren's thumb found the advance stud on the slate. She needed to know who had opened the trunk's inner seal before Nia reached it. The inner seal, Nia had reported, breached from the inside. Recent. That meant someone had been down there after Mara sealed it. Someone who knew the cache existed.

The recorder spun up. A click of old gears. Then static, thick and wet, like the sea pressing its mouth to the speaker.

A man's voice. Not Mara's.

It read like a cargo count. That was the first wrong thing — the man on the slate wasn't afraid, wasn't even fast. He spoke the way a diver speaks when he's rationing breath and refuses to spend a single word on panic.

"Mercy General, service level," the voice said. "Forty-two meters on the anchor line. There's a pocket here, air's holding. I've got hours. Longer, if I don't talk too much." A dry sound that might have been a laugh. "I'll talk too much."

Wren's thumb came off the advance stud. She knew that cadence. She'd rebuilt it a dozen times off other crews' slates — the flat, itemized calm of a man reading his own manifest while the water decides about him.

The static pressed in, thick and wet. Then he gave a date. Fourteen months gone.

"Deckhand logged aboard the Marrow as Adisa, Bayo," the voice said. "He's topside, on the drum. I can see the soles of his boots through the moon pool. Line's fouled on the second seal below the pharmacy. I asked him to re-rig it." A pause. The hiss filled it. "He said he would. He gave me his word."

Nobody on the Marrow moved. Up at the shutter Sol had gone still as a piling, one eye yet on the gate's red light, her jaw set hard enough to ache. Dey's head had come up off the mast step, the wet rattle in his chest gone quiet.

"Then he cut it," the voice said. Calm. Patient. "Clean. Above the knot, so it wouldn't snag going up. I watched the tail of it go through the moon pool. I'm in the pocket at forty-two meters, and I'm going to run out of hours in here." Another pause. "If anyone plays this back — the man who left me is Bayo Adisa. He'll tell you it was the surge. It wasn't the surge."

The recording clicked and wound down into hiss, and kept hissing, the barnacled speaker pushing dead sea-noise out into the cabin.

Wren had thumbed the stud to learn who opened the inner seal before Nia reached it. The slate had given her a different name instead, and above them the drum hauled on under its own power, load set, bearings biting the hull every turn — hauling up a girl who was spending the same kind of hours.

Then boots rang on the companionway.

Bayo climbed up into the light. Both hands were wrapped to the knuckle, the bandage gray and smeared with grease where he'd been feeding the line. He came up two rungs, saw every face in the cabin turned toward him and the slate hissing in Wren's lap, and stopped.

"Whose tape is that," he said. Still warm. Still smiling, the smile already reaching for whatever it needed to fix. "Sol. Sol, that's not —"

Wren's hand closed flat over the slate.

Wren didn't look up. Her thumb stayed on the advance stud, the slate's hiss filling the cabin like a held breath. "It's Salas's. From fourteen months ago. He named you, Bayo. He named you calm as a cargo count."

Bayo's smile didn't break. It softened, the corners pulling down into something that looked like regret and worked the same way — a tool, shaped for the job. "Wren. Love. You know me. I've made promises in worse air than this. I'll make it right. Let me take the drum. I'll haul her up myself. Penance, yeah? I owe the line."

He stepped forward, bandaged hands held out, palms up. The gray wrappings were stiff with salt and grease, the fingers swollen underneath. He'd been feeding line for hours, maybe days, the burns fresh enough to weep through the gauze.

Sol didn't move from the shutter. Her voice came flat, not loud. "You cut a man's line at forty-two meters and left him to breathe his last hours in a pocket. You stood on this drum and watched the tail go through the moon pool. Then you shipped out like nothing happened. You don't get penance. You get the shore."

"I'm not asking for shore," Bayo said. Still warm. Still low. "I'm asking for the line. Nia's on it. She's burning CO2 and the drum's eating bearings and Dey can't work it and Wren's on comms. Who else is there? You need a hand that knows the rhythm. I know the rhythm. I've held worse loads in worse surge. Let me hold this one."

Dey made a sound from the mast step — not a word, a wet choke of air through damaged lungs. His hands stayed white on the coil he couldn't turn.

Salas hadn't moved. The coil at his feet. The line wrapped on his forearm. His face was the gray of the water outside, eyes fixed on Bayo's bandaged hands.

Wren's voice came quiet, not rising. "You cut the line, Bayo. You *cut* it. Clean above the knot. He watched the tail go. Fourteen months he breathed in that pocket because you gave your word and then you cut it. What makes this load different?"

Bayo's smile thinned, stretched. "Because this one's *her*. Because I'm here. Because I'm asking." He looked at Sol, then Wren, then the drum where the line sang under tension. "Because if I don't hold it, the surge takes her before the drum finishes. You know the math. Twelve seconds between slams. The bearings are gone. The auto-haul'll jerk her on the next one. She needs a hand that feels it. I'm the only one left with two hands and the breath to use them."

He didn't deny it. Not once.

The drum groaned, a deep metal sound as the hull took a swell broadside. The line jumped, slack snapping tight, the carabiner screaming on the rail. Bayo's bandaged fingers twitched toward the drum's control lever.

"Get back," Sol said. "Now."

Bayo didn't move. "Captain. I'm not leaving this drum. Not while she's on the line. You can put me off at the gate. You can hand me to the Factor. But right now, *right now*, I'm the only thing between Nia and the bottom. Let me hold."

The surge hit. The Marrow rolled, the gate's red light sweeping the cabin at a crazy angle. The drum shuddered under the load. Bayo's hands found the lever, the brake, the rhythm — burned fingers closing on cold metal.

No one wanted the line-cutter's hands on the only line. But the drum was already his.

The drum didn't haul smooth. It bit and jerked, the hydrogen cell whining up to a scream as the surge caught the Marrow's quarter and heeled her hard, the line coming up at a crabbed angle through the moon pool, carabiner shrieking on the rail fairlead. Thirty-eight meters of wet rope and a girl who wasn't breathing right, and every revolution fought the hull's roll.

Dey's chest hitched, a wet whistle on the inhale, his hands clamped on the dead coil — he *wanted* the drum, his body remembered the rhythm even with his lungs gone to sponge, but the breath wouldn't come. He made the sound again, lower this time, a groan forced through narrowed airways, and his knuckles went bone-white.

Wren didn't look up from the comms. "Nia. Nia, can you hear —" Static. The carrier held. The return didn't. She keyed the mic again, thumb rigid on the transmit, voice stripped to the essential. "Drum to diver. Drum to diver. You're coming up. Stay with the line."

Sol braced one hand on the shutter frame, the other on the drum's emergency stop lever. The gate's red light swept the cabin at a drunken angle — the Marrow wallowing in the channel's confused chop, the storm tide pushing hard against the ebb. She cracked the shutter wider, cold air knifing in, and shouted over the cell's whine.

"Bayo! *Hold it steady*. No jerk, no surge-catch, you feel the load — you *hold*."

Bayo didn't turn. His bandaged hands moved on the controls, brake feathered, lever eased, the drum's rhythm finding a cruel sync with the hull's roll. Twelve seconds between slams. He counted them in his shoulders. The burns wept through the gauze, fresh blood darkening the gray wrappings where his fingers gripped metal.

"Holding, Captain," he said. Calm. Low. The same voice that had promised Salas a re-rigged line. "She's coming home."

The line snapped bar-tight. The carabiner rang like a struck bell. The drum stalled for a heartbeat — load peak, cell coughing — then the brake released a measured inch and the haul resumed, crooked and screaming.

Salas unfolded his arms. The coil at his feet stayed where it was, the bitter end still wrapped on his forearm, but his hands came up to the comms panel beside Wren — slow, deliberate, like a man placing a bet he's already lost. His fingers found the transmit key without looking. The burns on Bayo's hands were fresh. The burns in Salas's throat were fourteen months old.

He keyed the mic.

"Bayo."

One word. Flat. No volume, no edge, just the name dropped into the carrier wave like a weight into deep water. It rode the ship's comms down the shaft into the gray where Nia hung limp on the line, and up through the cracked shutter into the gate where Mara sat counting on the wet stair, and across the channel to any boat still listening on the open frequency.

The cabin didn't move. Bayo's hands didn't leave the controls. The drum kept its crooked rhythm, the hydrogen cell whining, the carabiner shrieking on the fairlead with every roll. But something in the air changed — the same shift that comes before a line parts, the sudden quiet where tension used to be.

Wren's thumb lifted from the transmit key. The static on the return channel didn't change. But three meters down, in water the color of old bruises, a fin blade caught current and drove — one kick, hard and clean, the motion of a body that had decided not to die yet.

The drum groaned. The load lightened by a fraction, just enough for the brake to catch a tooth. Bayo's bandaged fingers twitched on the lever, feeling it.

"Did you feel that," he said. Not a question. "She kicked."

Sol's hand came off the emergency stop lever. She didn't look at Salas. She didn't look at Bayo. Her eyes stayed on the line disappearing through the moon pool, watching for the next tell.

"Haul," she said. "Haul her home."
